title: Memory Bugs and How to Catch Them

scenes.say: A class that holds one hundred bytes can fail in five different ways. By the end, you'll find all five, explain each crash, and have a tool name the exact line.
Today you will do three things. Lose memory, and watch a leak happen. Break pointers four more ways: dangling, wild, use after delete, and double free. Then let a tool name the exact line.
lines: Let a tool name the exact line

scenes.title: Where did 100 bytes go?
scenes.statement: A function allocates 100 bytes with new[], then returns early. Nothing ever frees them.
scenes.say: Here is the problem. A function allocates one hundred bytes, then returns early. Nobody ever frees them. Where did those bytes go?

scenes.head: A coat check
scenes.say: Think of a coat check. The ticket in your hand is the pointer. The coat on the rack is the heap block. Lose the ticket, and the coat hangs there forever, unclaimable.

scenes.head: The early return
scenes.say: work allocates one hundred bytes, and d holds the address. If fail is true, we return early. The delete line is never reached. When work returns, d vanishes, but the heap block stays. Nobody holds its address, so nobody can ever free it. That is a leak.
Your turn. Now call work with true in a loop, a million times. What do you see? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: work(true) in a loop, 1,000,000 times. What happens?

scenes.head: Leaked memory, 100 bytes a call
scenes.say: Memory keeps climbing. A thousand calls leak about a tenth of a megabyte. A hundred thousand, ten megabytes. A million calls, a hundred megabytes. Only exit reclaims it, so servers suffer most.

scenes.head: Detect it with a tool
scenes.say: Leaks are silent, so use a tool. Compile with dash f sanitize equals address. Leak Sanitizer lists every block nobody can reach, at exit. Here: one hundred bytes, from line two.

output.text:
Direct leak of 100 byte(s) in 1 object(s) allocated from:
    #1 in work(bool) leak.cpp:2

setup.f: grep -E "Direct|work" | sed -E 's#.*ERROR#ERROR#; s# on .*##; s# at 0x.*##; s# 0x[0-9a-f]+##; s#/[^ ]*/##'

scenes.head: Prevent it: give it an owner
scenes.say: Prevention is ownership. Replace the raw pointer with a vector. Its destructor frees the memory on every exit, a return or an exception. For a single object, make unique. No new, no delete, no leak.

scenes.title: Which pointer is safe?
scenes.statement: q is a copy of p, and w was never set. After delete[] p, can you use p, q or w?

example.input: q = p; delete[] p; char* w;

scenes.say: Here is the problem. Pointer q is a copy of p, and w was never set. Now we delete p. Which of p, q and w are safe? None of them.

scenes.head: Street addresses
scenes.say: Think of street addresses. A dangling pointer is the address of a demolished house. A wild pointer is a scrawl you never wrote, a random address. And after delete, the lot may get a new house, so you walk into a stranger's home.

items.label: after delete
items.sub: the lot got a new owner

scenes.head: Two pointers, one delete
scenes.say: p points to the block, and q is a copy of that address. Delete p. The block is freed, but both pointers still hold its address. Setting p to null fixes p. But q still points at freed memory. That is a dangling pointer.

scenes.head: Other ways to dangle
scenes.say: Delete is not the only way. Return the address of a local, and x dies when the function returns. The compiler warns. Or keep a pointer into a vector, then push back. It may reallocate, moving every element, so first can point at freed memory.

output.text: warning: address of local variable ‘x’ returned [-Wreturn-local-addr]

scenes.head: A wild pointer
scenes.say: A wild pointer was never initialized. A local pointer holds whatever bits were on the stack, so the write lands somewhere unknown. Globals start as null. Locals and new memory do not. Dash Wall catches the easy cases.
Your turn. Look at that last code. A pointer never set, then written through. Is it dangling or wild? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `char* p;` never set, then `*p = 'x'`. Dangling or wild?

scenes.head: Wild versus dangling
scenes.say: Wild: never valid. Dangling: valid until the object died. Example: an unset local, versus a copy after delete. Catch it: dash Wall warns on wild ones, and sanitizers catch both.

scenes.title: Read it after delete
scenes.statement: p points to an int. delete p gives the block back. Then p is used again. What happens?
scenes.say: Here is the problem. A pointer p points to an int. We delete it, then use p anyway. What does the program do? Officially, anything.

scenes.head: The freed block gets a new owner
scenes.say: p points at forty two. Delete gives the block back. Then new int of ninety nine may reuse the very same block, so q points there. Now star p equals seven writes into q's int. Printing star q might show seven. No crash, just a wrong value.

scenes.head: Catch it at the line
scenes.say: Formally it is undefined, so the standard promises nothing. Address Sanitizer catches it at the exact line, and shows where the memory was freed. Line four read it, line three freed it.

output.text:
ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free
READ of size 1
    #0 in read() uaf.cpp:4

setup.f: grep -E "ERROR|READ|#0 .* in read" | sed -E 's#.*ERROR#ERROR#; s# on .*##; s# at 0x.*##; s# 0x[0-9a-f]+##; s#/[^ ]*/##'

scenes.say: Your turn. After delete p, you read star p. What does the standard promise about the value? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: What it can do
scenes.say: Nothing at all is promised. You may read the old value. You may read garbage. You may read another object's data. Or crash, maybe later. It often seems fine, a classic security hole.

scenes.title: Copy a Buffer, free it twice
scenes.statement: Buffer owns 100 bytes and frees them in its destructor. Copy one Buffer into another. What gets freed?
scenes.say: Here is the problem. Buffer owns one hundred bytes, and frees them in its destructor. We copy b1 into b2. Then both objects die. What gets freed?

scenes.head: A treasure map
scenes.say: Think of a treasure map. The map is the pointer, and the chest is the heap block. A shallow copy photocopies the map, not the chest. Both maps lead to one chest. The second owner finds an empty hole. A deep copy builds a second chest.

scenes.head: Copying an owner
scenes.say: b1 owns a block of one hundred bytes. Buffer b2 equals b1 uses the compiler's copy constructor, which copies the pointer, not the array. Now two objects think they own one block. At the end, b2 is destroyed first and frees the array. Then b1 deletes the same address again.

scenes.head: Double free, caught
scenes.say: Here is the whole class. The destructor deletes the array. The copy in copyIt shares it. Address Sanitizer reports attempting double free, in the destructor on line four, called from line nine.

output.text:
ERROR: AddressSanitizer: attempting double-free
    #1 in Buffer::~Buffer() buffer.cpp:4
    #2 in copyIt() buffer.cpp:9

setup.f: grep -E "ERROR|#[12] .* in (Buffer|copyIt)" | sed -E 's#.*ERROR#ERROR#; s# on .*##; s# at 0x.*##; s# 0x[0-9a-f]+##; s#/[^ ]*/##' | head -3

scenes.say: Your turn. Which change makes b2 independent, so each destructor frees its own block? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Buffer b2 = b1 frees twice. What is the real fix?

scenes.head: The fix: a deep copy
scenes.say: Write a copy constructor. It allocates a fresh block, and copies the bytes. Now each destructor frees its own block. Add a matching assignment operator too: that is the rule of three. Or delete copying, like unique pointer does.

scenes.head: Shallow versus deep
scenes.say: Copies: the pointer, versus the data. Afterwards: one shared block, versus one each. Destruction: double free, versus safe. Cost: cheap, versus an allocation. Hold a vector and you get deep copies free: the rule of zero.

scenes.title: Find the bug without guessing
scenes.statement: A program writes one int past the end of a 4-int heap array. Run normally, it seems fine.
scenes.say: Here is the problem. This program writes one past the end of a four int array. Normally it seems fine. We want the exact line.

scenes.head: A museum with alarm tape
scenes.say: Think of a museum. Every painting has alarm tape around it. Touch the tape, and the alarm rings. Address Sanitizer does the same: redzones around every heap block. It names the exact line.

scenes.head: How ASan sees the overflow
scenes.say: Each heap block gets poisoned redzones on both sides. A shadow map tracks which bytes are valid. The compiler checks it before every load and store. Our write to index four lands in the right redzone, and is caught. Freed memory is poisoned too, so use after free is caught. The cost: about two times slower.

scenes.head: ASan: the report
scenes.say: Compile with dash g and the sanitizer flag, then run. Address Sanitizer stops at the bad write. A heap buffer overflow, a write of four bytes, in overflow, line three.

output.text:
ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow
WRITE of size 4
    #0 in overflow() bug.cpp:3

setup.f: grep -E "ERROR|WRITE|#0 .* in overflow" | sed -E 's#.*ERROR#ERROR#; s# on .*##; s# at 0x.*##; s# 0x[0-9a-f]+##; s#/[^ ]*/##'

scenes.say: Your turn. You cannot rebuild the program. Which tool can still check the binary? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: No rebuild possible. Which tool still checks the binary?

scenes.head: Valgrind: no rebuild
scenes.say: Valgrind needs no rebuild. Add dash g for line numbers, and run the program under valgrind. It checks every memory access on a simulated processor. Here it reports the leak: one hundred bytes definitely lost. The catch: often twenty to thirty times slower. Never run an ASan build under it.

panels.code:
valgrind --leak-check=full ./app
# 100 bytes in 1 blocks are
# definitely lost

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: What is a memory leak? Heap memory still allocated, but unreachable. How do you detect it? Sanitizers, valgrind, or memory that keeps growing. How do you prevent it? Owners like vector and unique pointer, no raw new.
rows: heap memory still allocated, but unreachable

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Dangling pointer? An address whose object died, like a copy after delete. Wild pointer? Never initialized, so it holds garbage. Both are undefined to use. Avoid both? Initialize everything, use smart pointers, and turn on dash Wall.
rows: address of a dead object, e.g. a copy after `delete`

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: What happens after delete? Undefined behavior. The block may be reused, so a write corrupts another object, with no crash. How do you catch it? Address Sanitizer names the line. Prevent it with smart pointers.
rows: ASan names the line; smart pointers

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Double free? One block released twice. Usual cause? Copying a class that owns a raw pointer. Shallow versus deep? Pointer copied, versus data copied. Fix? A deep copy, rule of three, or a vector.
rows: copying a class that owns a raw pointer

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: How do you detect memory corruption? Address Sanitizer: compile with the flag. Or Valgrind: no rebuild, but much slower. Both find overflows, use after free, and leaks. Run them in tests.
rows: no rebuild; simulated CPU; much slower
overflows, use-after-free, leaks: run in CI

scenes.head: Practice before your interview
scenes.say: Solve these next. LeetCode two thirty seven, delete node in a linked list: free the removed node. LeetCode one thirty eight, copy list with random pointer: a deep copy. LeetCode one thirty three, clone graph: deep copy with cycles.
rows: LeetCode 237 · Delete Node in a Linked List
LeetCode 138 · Copy List with Random Pointer

scenes.say: So say this. A leak is memory nobody can reach. Dangling, wild, freed, and double freed pointers are all undefined behavior. Give every block one owner, and let sanitizers name the line.
lines: Leak: memory nobody can reach any more.
Dangling, wild, freed, double-freed: all UB.
One owner per block. Let ASan name the line.
